newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Gore announce Internet grants, hookups.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Gore announce Internet grants, hookups.

text.p: WASHINTON, Feb 9 - President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore teamed up electronically on Saturday to report a major advance in hooking up U.S. schools to the Internet and to announce federal grants to speed the process.
Co-starring with Clinton on the president's weekly radio broadcast, Gore said the Department of Education would award Technology Literacyinois, Mississippi and New Mexico.
The grants are the first under a programme that will spend $200 million this year, and more than double that amount in 1998 if Congress approves Clinton's budget proposal.
"Communities will use these funds to equip classrooms with computers, link schools to the Internet and train teachers in new information technologies," the vice president said.
In the next breath of the five-minute radio chat, Clin percent of U.S. schools were now connected to the Internet -- one of the main lanes of the so-called "Information Highway."

His goal is to have every American school and library linked to the Internet by the year 2000 to enable students to rapinton said the Internet connection rate was "almost double the number of schools connected in 1994," and that he would not rest until the job was completed.

"To give our children the best education, we must help them to harness the powerful forces of technology," he said. "For the first time in history, children in the most isolated rural towns, the most comfortable suburbs and the poorest inner city schools will have the same access to the same universe of knowledge."
Clinton said in his State of the Union speech laone second-term priority. Gore said passage of the Telecommunications Act last year would help move the country into the information age.

Liberal critics of the new law claim its initial effects are anything but encouraging however. Instead of increasing the free flow of information, they say it has enabled media giants to expand their holdings, giving a relative handful of firms enormous power to control what Americans see and hear.
